scenes.text: Here are the two investments from the end of the last video, one in each jar. Ten thousand dollars at six per cent a year, for ten years. The only difference is one phrase. Simple interest pays six per cent of the original amount every year, so the account grows by the same six hundred dollars each time. That's an arithmetic model, and after ten years it's sixteen thousand dollars. Compound interest pays six per cent of the current balance, so each year multiplies it by one point zero six. That's a geometric model, and after ten years it's seventeen thousand, nine hundred and eight dollars, forty-eight. Same numbers, different words, different model. So which words justify which model?

Here are the finance phrases to look for. The same amount added each period means an arithmetic model, a straight line. The same percentage of the current amount means a geometric model, multiplying by one plus r each period. Equal end-of-period deposits into an account that starts at zero add up to a geometric series, so that's an annuity, with future value M times one plus r to the n, minus one, all over r. And equal repayments on a loan, where interest is charged on the balance, give the loan model, with the balance zero when it's paid off. In every one, r is the rate for one period, and n counts the periods. Which model does "can afford a repayment each month" point to? Think for three seconds. It's a loan with equal repayments.

So here's that question. A buyer can afford two thousand eight hundred dollars a month, at four point eight per cent a year, compounded monthly, for twenty-five years. What's the most they can borrow? Per month, r is point zero zero four, and n is three hundred. The loan is paid off after the last repayment, so set the balance after three hundred months to zero. The unknown this time is P, the amount borrowed. Move the repayments' part to the other side and divide, and P is about four hundred and eighty-eight thousand, six hundred and fifty-eight dollars, seventy-nine. Because it's a maximum, round down, to seventy-eight cents, so the repayments are sure to clear it. Multiplying two thousand eight hundred by three hundred is the classic slip. That's the total repaid, including all the interest.

Probability questions work the same way. If the question lists the values with their probabilities, it's a discrete distribution, and the probabilities add to one. If it gives a density function, probabilities are areas under it, and the total area is one. If equal-width parts of an interval are equally likely, the density is flat, one over the width of the interval. And if it says normally distributed, with a mean and a standard deviation, the curve is a bell, and the empirical rule or z-scores give the probabilities. Here's a test. A question asks how likely a delivery is to take more than fifty-eight minutes. Which model fits? Think for three seconds. You can't tell yet. The question has to say which shape it means.

First, suppose the time is uniform from forty to sixty minutes, so equal stretches of time are equally likely. The density is flat, at one over twenty. More than fifty-eight minutes is the last two minutes of the twenty, so the probability is two twentieths, which is one in ten. Now suppose instead the times are normally distributed, with mean fifty and standard deviation four. Fifty-eight is two standard deviations above the mean. About ninety-five per cent of times are within two standard deviations, so about five per cent are outside, and half of that is above. That's about two point five per cent. Same threshold, different shape, so a different answer. And the normal model isn't even limited to forty to sixty. The normal curve piles its probability near the mean, and leaves only a thin tail out there.

One more pair. In the first question, a spinner lands on one, two, three or four, with probability k x. In the second, X is a choc chip's distance from the centre of a cookie, in centimetres, and it has density k x, from zero to four. Same rule, but is k the same? For the list, the four probabilities add to one. That's k plus two k plus three k plus four k, which is ten k, so k is one tenth. For the density, the area under k x from zero to four is one. That's a triangle, half of four times four k, which is eight k, so k is one eighth, the cookie's density from the earlier video. A sum of bars and an area under a line are different totals, so they give different values of k.
Here's the habit for every model question. The words pick the model, and the numbers just fill it in. Same amount, add. Same percentage, multiply. A list sums to one. A density has area one.

Your turn. Two thousand dollars is deposited at the end of each year into a new, empty account earning five per cent a year, compounded annually. Find the value of the account immediately after the tenth deposit. Pause here to answer.

Equal end-of-year deposits, starting from zero, make an annuity. The last one goes in at the end, so it earns nothing yet. So the value is two thousand, times one point zero five to the ten, minus one, all over point zero five. That's about twenty-five thousand, one hundred and fifty-five dollars, seventy-nine. Thirty-two thousand, five hundred and seventy-seven dollars, eighty-nine is wrong. It treats all ten deposits as if they went in at the start.

Last one. Bags of chips are filled by a machine, and their masses are normally distributed, with mean five hundred grams and standard deviation five grams. Use the empirical rule to estimate the percentage of bags under four hundred and ninety grams. Pause here to answer.

Four hundred and ninety is ten grams below the mean, which is two standard deviations. About ninety-five per cent of bags are within two standard deviations, so about five per cent are outside. Only the lower tail counts, so it's about two point five per cent. Five per cent is wrong. It counts both tails, the heavy bags as well.

So in every model question, read the words before the numbers. That's the last of the practice videos, and the end of the Year 12 Advanced course. Here are the three habits, one for differentiation, one for integration and one for models.
Here are the key notes. Pause the video if you need more time to copy them.
